title: What does a 1:N model of a cargo UAV tell you about the 1:1 aircraft?
lede: research programme (proposal stage): per-quantity error budget for a Froude-scaled cargo aircraft model, with a stdlib scaling calculator; first-order result: at 1:10 the model needs 17 to 35% more power than Froude scaling predicts
summary: An open research programme on sub-scale flight testing of cargo and delivery aircraft. Dynamic (Froude) scaling keeps trim, mode frequencies and gust response, but Reynolds number falls as n<sup>1.5</sup>, so skin friction rises, and cell, motor and propeller performance do not scale with the airframe. The programme asks how large each error is for 1:2 to 1:20 models of an electric cargo aircraft, and whether a corrected model can recover it. Milestone 1 is a stdlib calculator (9 tests; exponent table dimensionally checked, ISA and Sutherland values checked) and a first-order flat-plate result for a 1,000 kg, aspect-ratio-10 airframe: at 1:10 the model needs 1.27× the Froude-scaled power (1.17 to 1.35 across form-factor, wetted-area and aspect-ratio sweeps) and L/D falls from 22.8 to 18.0. An untripped laminar-flow variant makes small models look better than full size, which is a modelling artefact and the reason the next milestones use XFOIL polars measured against UIUC data. The airframe constants are design choices, not a specific aircraft; the Froude exponents and the NASA TP-1435 and other citations are from memory and were not machine-checked (registries returned 403). Preliminary. Milestone 6a: on 134 measured cruise flights of a DJI Matrice 100 (Rodrigues et al. 2022 data, CC BY 4.0), electrical power scales with takeoff mass to the power 1.54 (95% bootstrap interval 1.41 to 1.67 over flights), consistent with the m<sup>1.5</sup> behind Froude power n<sup>3.5</sup>, within one airframe and a 13.6% mass range; electrical cruise power is 1.85× the ideal induced power at every payload, and falls 10% from 4 to 12 m/s. Payload is partly confounded with flight day (density not logged). Milestone 7a: at n = 0.2 the uncorrected model needs 1.157× the Froude power; a search of 178 section and boundary-layer cases (NACA 4-digit and low-Reynolds sections, CL within 6%, lift-curve slope within 5%) reaches at best 1.086, so no section restores it to within 5% (H5 refuted in this space; NeuralFoil polars, similarity kept). Milestone 11a (airspace): for one delivery hub in Manhattan with 17,250 measured destinations (NYC Uber pickups, April 2014; CC BY 4.0), 20 m/s cruise and a 50 m separation radius, en-route losses of separation per flight grow linearly with traffic and reach 0.1 per flight at 62 flights/h in one layer. A closed form derived from the radial geometry, C = (λ<sup>2</sup>/v) E[min(2 min(d<sub>1</sub>, d<sub>2</sub>), R / sin(Δφ/2))], matches an exact closest-approach simulator within 1% in the base case and within 4.3% in 89 of 90 sweep comparisons. Manhattan's narrow bearings double the conflicts; the gas model is 7× low (17× at 10 km); separate outbound and inbound layers remove 95%. Speed and separation radius swept, not sourced; no wind or other operators. Milestone 11b (wind): a generalised closed form (within 1.7% of the simulator in 8 base cases) shows wind raises one layer’s en-route conflicts by about as much as it lengthens time aloft, v/H = √(1 − w<sup>2</sup> sin<sup>2</sup>β)/(1 − w<sup>2</sup>); over 4,392 measured ERA5 100 m wind hours (NYC, Apr to Sep 2014) the average hour adds 6.1% at 20 m/s (10.0% at 15, 2.7% at 30), and the outbound/inbound layer split still leaves under 1% at equal airspeeds. Steady wind per hour; preliminary. Milestone 11c (several hubs and operators): one operator’s nearest-hub flights never cross (zero cross-hub conflicts; en-route conflicts per flight fall from 0.40 to 0.023 going from 1 to 8 hubs at 240 flights/h); with four overlapping operators 31.5% of en-route conflicts are crossings, a closed form with a crossing term matches the simulator within 7.4%, and the semicircular altitude rule leaves 68% fewer en-route conflicts than an outbound/inbound split. Straight legs, equal speeds, k-means operator sites; preliminary. Milestone 11e (which bit to spend extra altitude layers on): with four overlapping operators, separating the operators whose service areas overlap most, on top of the semicircular rule, leaves 2.3× to 3.7× fewer en-route conflicts than separating outbound from inbound legs, and a speed band does worse than leg direction; the closed form picks a tied-best assignment in all three scenarios. Leg direction still wins once conflicts within 250 m of a hub are counted. Illustrative speeds and shares; preliminary. Milestone 11f (eight operators, which share a layer): max-cut on closed-form pairwise conflict weights picks the simulator’s best of all 127 two-group splits in all three scenarios and, on top of the semicircular rule, leaves 20% to 29% of its en-route conflicts; max-cut on market share over hub distance is within 2.2% with no traffic model, a demand-overlap split is 1.3× to 1.6× worse and a speed split 1.5× to 2.7× worse. Illustrative speeds and shares; preliminary. Milestone 11g (24 random layouts, mixed radii, speeds and shares): the closed-form max-cut stays within 1.6% of the simulator’s best split in all 24, while the hub-distance heuristic is at least 5% worse in 19 of 24 (median 1.14×, worst 1.75×), so 11f’s near-free heuristic held only for equal-radius operators. Swept, not sourced; preliminary.
